title: Starting a Business · Episode 2
chapters: Why we pay more for a name
Cash flow: the lifeblood of business

units.t: Starting a Business. Episode two.
In this episode: Why we pay more for a name, The hidden psychology of prices and Cash flow: the lifeblood of business.
Part one. Why we pay more for a name.
In blind taste tests, people often cannot tell their favourite cola from its rival.
So why will they happily pay more for the logo?
From cattle to confidence.
Long before logos, farmers burned marks into the hides of cattle to show whose they were.
The modern brand grew out of the Industrial Revolution, when goods travelled far from their makers.
Buy flour from a neighbour and you knew who to blame if it was bad.
If it came from a distant factory, a trusted name on the packet did that job.
In 1876 the Bass brewery's red triangle became the first trade mark registered under a new British law.
Brands also act as mental shortcuts.
A large supermarket stocks thousands of products, so a familiar name lets you assume the product will match last time.
Much of what a brand sells is confidence, which is why travellers often pick a global chain over an unknown local cafe.
The cola experiment.
In the 1970s Pepsi ran the Pepsi Challenge, a marketing campaign built on blind taste tests in which many people preferred Pepsi.
Yet Coca-Cola stayed the bigger seller.
In 2004, neuroscientists explored why.
When people tasted the drinks without knowing which was which, their preferences were fairly evenly split.
When told they were drinking Coke, more said they preferred it, and brain scans showed extra activity in areas linked to memory and emotion.
The brand was not just a label on the can.
A lifetime of advertising, memories and associations had become part of the experience of drinking it.
Brands work partly in our heads, and that is still real to us.
Status and signalling.
In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen coined the phrase conspicuous consumption for wealthy people spending lavishly to display status.
Luxury brands still trade on this idea.
A handbag with a famous logo holds the same things as an unbranded one, but it also sends a message.
For some luxury goods, raising the price can even increase demand, because the high price is part of the appeal.
Economists sometimes call these Veblen goods.
Signalling is not only about wealth.
People choose brands to show they are outdoorsy, ethical, sporty or creative.
A sticker on a laptop or a logo on a pair of runners can quietly announce which group you feel you belong to.
When brands become words.
Escalator, thermos and trampoline all began as brand names.
People came to use them for any product of that type, and in some countries the owners lost exclusive rights to the name.
Courts call this genericide.
In the United States, Otis lost its trade mark on escalator in 1950.
Companies fight to avoid this fate, which is why some insist on phrases like Band-Aid brand adhesive bandages.
In Australia, Esky is a registered trade mark, even though many people use it for any portable cooler.
The irony is painful for owners: becoming a household word is the ultimate marketing success, yet it can wipe out the legal value of the name.
Brands under pressure.
Own brands once had a plain, cheap reputation.
When Aldi arrived in Australia in 2001, it built its business largely on own-label products sold at low prices.
Coles and Woolworths expanded their own ranges in response.
Many home brand items come from similar factories to branded goods, sometimes the same manufacturers.
Well-known brands must now justify higher prices with quality, innovation or emotional appeal, not familiarity alone.
Because a brand is really a reputation, it is fragile.
Decades of trust can be damaged by one scandal, unsafe product or misleading conduct, and sales and share prices can fall sharply.
Some brands recover by acting quickly and honestly.
For shoppers, the lesson is to check whether a product earns its extra price.
The key idea: Brands began as marks of ownership and now act as mental shortcuts that reduce the risk of a bad choice.
Part two. The hidden psychology of prices.
Why does almost everything cost $9.
99, and why does a menu include a dish nobody orders?
Prices are quietly designed to steer your choices.
Numbers that nudge.
A price of $4.
99 is only one cent under $5, yet it feels like four dollars and something.
This is the left-digit effect: we read left to right and give the first digit extra weight.
Sales data show prices ending in 9 can lift demand, though it varies by product.
Luxury shops often use round prices like $500 instead, because a price that looks discounted can make an expensive item feel cheap.
The first number you see also works as an anchor.
A jacket marked Was $400, now $199 feels cheap whether or not anyone paid $400.
In 1970s experiments, Tversky and Kahneman showed estimates were nudged by a number from a spun wheel.
In Australia, was prices must be genuine, and the ACCC has acted against misleading ones.
The decoy nobody buys.
Behavioural economist Dan Ariely described an old subscription offer from The Economist: web access for $59, print for $125, or print plus web for $125.
Nobody sensible picks print alone when the bundle costs the same, so why include it?
Because it makes the bundle look like a steal.
When Ariely tested the offer on students, most chose the bundle.
When he removed the print-only option, far more chose the cheaper web-only deal.
This is called the decoy effect.
You will see it in cinema popcorn sizes, coffee cups and phone plans, where a middle option is priced to push you towards the largest one.
Different prices, same thing.
Two people sitting side by side on a plane may have paid wildly different fares.
Economists call this price discrimination, and it is often legal.
The aim is to charge each customer close to what they are willing to pay.
Airlines do it with booking dates and flexible tickets.
Cinemas do it with cheap Tuesday sessions.
Software companies offer student discounts, because students have little money now but may become loyal paying customers.
Coupons and loyalty apps work similarly: people who collect points or hunt for codes tend to be more price sensitive, so they get a lower price while everyone else pays full price.
The product barely changes, but the price fits the customer.
Making paying painless.
Zero is special.
Shoppers often choose a free item over a better deal that costs a little, because free removes any sense of risk or loss.
Freemium apps are free to download and earn money from the few users who pay for extras.
Free shipping thresholds work too: if delivery is free over $50 and your cart is at $43, many people add something rather than pay a few dollars postage.
Paying also hurts a little, more with cash than cards and less still when money leaves automatically.
That is why subscriptions have spread.
$15 a month feels lighter than $180 a year, and inertia keeps people paying for services they rarely use.
Review your bank statement every few months and cancel anything you would not sign up for again today.
Seeing through the tricks.
None of these techniques are secret, and once you know them they lose some power.
A useful defence is unit pricing.
Large Australian supermarkets must display unit prices, such as the cost per 100 grams, which makes it easier to compare a big pack with a small one, or a brand with a home brand.
Another defence is to decide what something is worth to you before you see the price tag, so an anchor cannot do your thinking for you.
The ACCC has also cracked down on drip pricing, where extra fees appear only at the end of a purchase.
If a price seems misleading, the ACCC website explains your rights and how to report it.
The key idea: Prices ending in 9 feel cheaper because we weigh the first digit most, and a high first price anchors our judgement.
Part three. Cash flow: the lifeblood of business.
A business can be profitable on paper and still run out of money.
Understanding why is one of the most important lessons in business.
Profit is not cash.
Profit is revenue minus expenses over a period, and under standard accounting it's recorded when a sale is made, not when the money arrives.
Cash flow is the actual timing of money entering and leaving your bank account.
You can make a $10,000 sale in March, book the profit, and not see the money until June.
In the meantime you still have to pay rent, wages, suppliers and tax.
Profit keeps score; cash keeps the lights on.
Why profitable firms fail.
A business can fail while its sales are growing.
Imagine a manufacturer that wins a big order.
It must buy materials and pay staff for months, while the customer pays 60 days after delivery.
If cash runs out in between, it may be unable to pay its debts on time, even though the order is profitable.
Growth that outpaces available cash is sometimes called overtrading.
The length of this loop is the cash conversion cycle: cash goes into stock or labour, becomes a sale, then waits to be paid.
A cafe paid at the counter has a short cycle.
A builder who invoices weeks later needs far more cash to keep going.
Many small business advisers cite cash flow as a common reason small businesses struggle or close.
Managing cash in and out.
Late payments are a common drain.
Invoice as soon as work is done, not at month's end.
Make invoices clear: what was delivered, the amount, the due date and easy payment options.
If you're registered for GST, invoices must meet tax invoice requirements, which the ATO explains.
Consider shorter terms, deposits for large jobs or progress payments, and follow up politely but promptly.
Outflows matter too.
Pay suppliers on time, but there's usually no need to pay weeks early.
Avoid tying up cash in excess stock.
The classic trap is tax: GST you collect isn't your money, and neither is income tax you'll owe later.
Many owners move a set percentage of each payment into a separate account.
Runway and forecasting.
Runway is vital for new businesses not yet profitable.
Divide your cash by your monthly net cash outflow, or burn rate.
With $60,000 in the bank and $10,000 more going out than coming in each month, you have about six months.
Knowing this early gives you time to cut costs, raise prices, chase sales or find funding.
A forecast can be a simple spreadsheet.
List cash coming in, based on when customers will realistically pay, not when you invoice.
List cash going out: wages, rent, suppliers, loans, super, GST and tax.
The difference gives a running balance.
Many businesses keep a rolling 13-week forecast, updated weekly.
The goal isn't perfect prediction; it's spotting dips in time to act.
Healthy cash habits.
A few habits make a big difference.
Look at your bank balance and unpaid invoices every week.
Build a cash buffer, with many advisers suggesting enough to cover at least a few months of fixed costs.
Keep business and personal money in separate accounts.
Use accounting software to track who owes you and what you owe.
If cash is getting tight, act early.
Talk to your accountant, your bank and, if needed, the ATO about payment arrangements.
This is general information only; a registered tax agent or accountant can advise on your situation.
The key idea: Profit measures earnings over a period, while cash flow tracks when money actually moves in and out.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did brands become more important during the Industrial Revolution?
Answer. Goods travelled far from their makers.
Question two. What is the left-digit effect?
Answer. Giving the first digit extra weight.
Question three. How can a business record a profit yet have no cash?
Answer. Profit is booked at the sale, but payment arrives later.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
